en: The Rafflesia consueloae, discovered in the Philippine rainforest, produces a massive flower that can weigh up to eleven kilograms.
The Philippine tarsier has enormous eyes that are actually larger than its brain, helping it hunt insects in the dark.
The Philippine eagle has a large, shaggy crest on its head that it raises to communicate with other eagles.
The Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park in the Sulu Sea protects over six hundred species of fish and coral.
The tamaraw, a dwarf buffalo endemic to Mindoro, has short, V-shaped horns that point backward to help it navigate dense forests.
The Philippine Department of Health officially recognizes the lagundi plant's leaves as an effective natural remedy for coughs.
Filipino farmers raise milkfish, locally called bangus, in coastal pens where the fish feed on natural algae and plankton.
The abaca plant, native to the Philippines, produces exceptionally strong fibers from its leaf stalks used to make Manila rope.
The Philippine crocodile is a freshwater reptile endemic to the country that is currently critically endangered due to habitat loss.
Mangrove forests in Pampanga have specialized stilt roots that anchor the trees in soft mud and filter salt from seawater.
The Aedes aegypti mosquito, which breeds in stagnant water around Filipino homes, transmits the dengue virus to humans.
The waling-waling, known as the queen of Philippine orchids, grows high on tree branches to capture sunlight in dense forests.
